turns.prompt_text: What is composting? I have plenty of chicken bones. I would like to compost but I don't know how
turns.response_html:
Composting is the natural process of recycling organic matter—like food scraps and yard waste—into a nutrient-rich soil amendment often called "black gold". By providing a controlled environment for bacteria, fungi, and other organisms, you turn waste into fertilizer that improves soil health and reduces landfill contributions.

Can You Compost Chicken Bones?

Yes, but they are considered "advanced" composting material. Because bones are dense, they take a long time to break down and can attract pests (rats, raccoons) if not handled correctly.

In a standard backyard bin, bones often remain intact for months or years. To compost them effectively, use one of these three approaches:

1. The "Bokashi" Method (Recommended for Beginners)

Bokashi is an anaerobic (airtight) fermentation system that uses specialized microbes to "pickle" food waste, including bones, meat, and dairy.

  • How it works: You place food scraps in a sealed bucket and sprinkle them with "bokashi bran" (inoculated with microbes).
  • Why use it: It processes bones much faster than traditional composting. After fermenting for a few weeks, the bones will be soft enough to bury in your garden soil, where they will fully decompose.

2. Hot Composting

If you maintain a large, active compost pile, you can break down bones, but it requires strict temperature management.

  • Temperature: Your pile must consistently reach 135°F to 160°F to kill pathogens and break down proteins.
  • Technique: Remove all remaining meat from the bones first (meat attracts pests). Place the bones in the very center of the pile, where heat is highest.
  • Preparation: Boiling bones for stock first makes them brittle and significantly faster to decompose.

3. Municipal or Industrial Composting

This is the easiest path if available. Many city-run green waste programs use industrial-scale high-heat facilities designed specifically to handle meat, dairy, and bones. Check your local municipality’s waste management website to see if they accept "food scraps" or "organics" in your curbside bin.

Basic Composting Principles

If you are starting a general compost pile for your fruit and vegetable scraps, follow the "Browns and Greens" rule:

  • Greens (Nitrogen): Provides protein for microbes. Examples: vegetable peels, fruit scraps, coffee grounds, grass clippings.
  • Browns (Carbon): Provides energy and structure. Examples: dry leaves, shredded cardboard, straw, twigs, sawdust.
  • Balance: Aim for a ratio of roughly 3 parts Brown to 1 part Green by volume.
  • Maintenance: Keep the pile damp (like a wrung-out sponge) and turn it occasionally with a pitchfork to introduce oxygen.
